Canada who did not even know when they were pregnant. That is how much they knew about their bodies.
I want to challenge the members of this House to say that this is no longer acceptable, that we will save costs and save lives by implementing family planning, education and sexually transmitted disease education programs now.
I urge all members of this House to vote in favour of this motion.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member's speech, and I know she is very concerned, very interested and very articulate on matters that concern women, family planning and children's issues.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit I am not sufficiently familiar with the programs that exist in other Canadian provinces as they relate to the services available to people in various locations. I am familiar with the programs in Quebec, and although there are a number of shortcomings, I believe that in Quebec, with our network of LCSCs, we have some very useful programs that serve Quebec families very well.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government is fully aware of the need for effective programs for sex education and family planning, especially for young people. And speaking of young people, not long ago, a pilot project was launched, which the hon. member may not have heard about, and this project has now been started in the LCSCs and deals with prevention of sexually transmitted diseases, AIDS and, of course, teenage pregnancies. There is some rather innovative material which I have not seen yet. I only saw the adds that appeared in the various media which mentioned a brochure that, I am told, speaks in a veiy direct style to young people, to make them realize that their health is at stake, and that this is for them. I think we should all have a look at this material.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member may not know that in 1977, there was a conference of provincial health ministers, and they declared unanimously, at a federal-provincial meeting, that family planning services came under provincial jurisdiction.
Private Members' Business
After this declaration in 1977, the role and impact of the Canadian Federation for Planned Parenthood and even the Serena Group started to shrink somewhat.
Mr. Speaker, I have a lot of notes here, but I would like to stick to the essentials. Responsibility does not lie exclusively with the State. I think the churches, provincial governments, volunteer groups working in our ridings and all Canadians should stop playing hide and seek and start speaking openly about these matters to the young people we meet.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Federation for Planned Parenthood has done remarkable work since 1955, because it set the scene for a host of provincial volunteer organizations to start dealing with the important question of family planning.
That being said, I will admit, and I agree more or less with the hon. member-it is a personal matter-after the debate we had on the Abortion Bill, it was said repeatedly by the people and groups that came to testify before the committee that there was a great need for information and family planning and prevention.
Today, we have a federal-provincial system. The hon. member for the New Democratic Party is in favour of a strong central government, if I am not mistaken. That is her view of Canada, and it is her right to have this vision of Canada. Personally, there should be a division. We must have programs administered by the provinces who are in a better position to know how to serve the target population. As you know, education is exclusively a provincial matter. Now I think that a family planning program must be pursued in cooperation with the Department of Education and the Department of Health. The federal government could use its spending power to help the provinces set up such programs, which have become absolutely necessary.
Mr. Speaker, I often wonder about it because a great deal of documentation exists and much has been done. It seems absolutely incredible to me that in 1991 we face such an alarming number of unwanted pregnancies. The hon. member mentioned the number of abortions performed in Canada. I agree with her and I also think that women must be able to choose whether or not to have an abortion, which is an extremely difficult choice, as we know.

October 31, 1991
Private Members' Business
The Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada receives a $146,000 grant. That may not seem like much, it is true, but with that statement by provincial health ministers at a federal-provincial conference, the provinces now have programs and I think they have some good ones. As I said earlier, we obviously need research on reproductive health throughout Canada. The government set up a royal commission of inquiry on reproductive methods that I hope will give us good results. The minister responsible for the status of women also made an announcement concerning a national study on violence against women and violence against children.
Mr. Speaker, I know that my time is nearly up. You know that as members of Parliament, we are all amazed at the tremendous work done by volunteers in our ridings. You know that volunteers do a remarkable job in community health, hospitals and local community service centres. We often cannot find words to express how much we owe to these many Canadians who give their time. Certainly national organizations like Serena and the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada should receive more funding to help the provinces, groups and volunteers throughout the country set up good prevention programs for young people, because I think the situation has become a tragedy to which we cannot remain insensitive.
I hope that the government can play a leading role, but with the help and support of the provinces and the youth protection branches in the various social service systems. For example, the Laurentian region has the youth protection branch in St. Jerome. In short, a whole series of organizations should get together to come up with a good policy that I think should begin in early childhood, in the schools. We should stop being afraid of calling a spade a spade and tell children the facts, tell them from their first days in school that drugs and sexual abuse are intolerable and that the problems related to sexually transmitted diseases are serious. If these children are educated about it from a young age, I think that we could have results. But I must say that parents have to be convinced that it is necessary and through concerted effort we can do that.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker-you are indicating to me that my time is up-by again congratulating the hon.
member for New Westminster-Burnaby who moved the motion. I encourage her and my colleagues in all parties in the House to continue trying to solve this serious problem so that in future our young people will know what it is about before they have sexual relations.

Mr. Speaker, it is with somewhat mixed feelings that I rise today to give my strongest support to this motion of my hon. friend from New Westminster-Burnaby.
I support her motion in every way possible. I underscore and underline everything she said with regard to the drastic importance of reinstating the family planning division at Health and Welfare Canada, reinstating funding to Planned Parenthood of Canada and, perhaps most important, establishing new programs to combat sexually transmitted diseases and unwanted pregnancies.
I appreciate the remarks of the hon. parliamentary secretary. I think, in a non-partisan way, I know where she stands on many of these issues as well. I know there have been issues that have been very divisive in this House, that have split all our caucuses. Sometimes it has been hard for women on all sides of the House regarding certain issues, particularly those relating more specifically to questions of gender and sexuality, but I appreciate the hon. parliamentary secretary's beliefs and statements.
However, I have to take a little exception to what she says not in the pure philosophical sense, but in the practical sense. It is with regard to the question of volunteers and programming.
I would be the first to admit that in the area of social programs Quebec probably leads the nation, but it does not deny the statistics that Quebec has the highest rate of unwanted pregnancies. It does not deny the statistics that there is, and I stand here as a Catholic and say this, a connection between religion and these unhappy statistics. If we think that we can solve this very deep-rooted problem through a volunteer program we are dreaming. I think the only thing that is going to solve this problem is direct government action.
Some of that government action can come from the provincial governments and some of it can come from the federal government, but the federal government,



particularly with regard to provinces such as the hon. parliamentary secretary's and my own, will have a dual role to play because of the funding necessary for provincial governments to put in place in my province and in the province of Quebec such programs as we are talking about.
I think our problem goes even deeper than that because although we are in the 1990s, if I can say that Canada and Canadian society is still sicklied o'er, if you will, with a pale hue of Victoriana. We still refuse to come to grips as governments, provincial or federal, with questions of sexuality. There is this left over idea somewhere that if we keep on ignoring it, it will go away.
The hon. parliamentary secretary and the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby and I suffered, and I use that word advisedly, through the legislative committee on Bill C-43. We suffered abuse, we suffered insults, we suffered threats and we suffered, I think, as women parliamentarians trying to deal with the legislative response. If I overstep I apologize to the parliamentary secretary, but I think that not one of us felt what we did was really adequate in the long run.
I think that we have a unique opportunity through a motion such as this one to look at the root of the problem and try to solve it at the root where it belongs. There is not a woman in this House, I doubt in this country, I doubt a woman in this world, who is in favour of abortion. To each one of us, on a personal level, it is a terrible option, but for a number of women it is the only option and it is the only option because governments have not acted, because governments have not put money in place for programs to educate.
Someone once said to me in a debate some years ago that I thought education was the answer to everything. I want to say that I guess I plead guilty to that accusation because if education is not the answer then I fear there is no answer, but I refuse to believe that.
We have to look at the question of education and the tools to give young people, and I agree again with the parliamentary secretary that you have to start at a very early age. We have to ensure that there are family life programs at every age level. My own personal idea, and I have held this idea for some time, is that the federal government could contribute significantly to the educa-
Private Members' Business
tional side without getting into a jurisdictional hassle with the provinces if it looked at some sort of national advertising program.
We have seen, and it has been done by the province of Ontario, it has been done by other provincial governments as well as the federal government, advertising campaigns that can be fairly explicit and that will have an impact.
Twenty years ago, as a university student, I was a resident's assistant and many of the younger students would come to me with questions. I was absolutely appalled at the level of ignorance they held about their own bodies, about procreation, about biology. What horrifies me even more today is that while in some areas through some school programs, through some public education, we have managed to alleviate that ignorance a little bit, there is more ignorance out there in a broader and a more dangerous sense.
The ignorance about sexually transmitted diseases, for example, and not just AIDS which kills but also other venereal diseases such as gonorrhoea which leaves women chronically ill, chronically infertile, in chronic pain and so on, is absolutely appalling. Yet we do nothing as a national government to combat it.
I use as an example the programs that were put in place by provincial governments to deal with impaired driving. That is one example. I do not say it is the only example but it is a start.
I refer back to what I said about the Victorian mindset that still holds Canada in a death grip. I use the term "death grip" advisedly. We are not prepared to say to our young people: "Yes, we understand that your sexuality drives you, particularly strongly the younger you are, in your teens and in your early twenties". We throw them out into this kind of a world with a great number of people saying: "Just say no". Just saying no does not work. Just saying no does not answer the question. What has to answer the question are national programs and a national commitment to assist provinces on the educational level and on the funding level for family planning and education.
If we do not do that, then the lives it is going to cost will be laid at our doorstep.

Private Members' Business

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to compliment the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby on her initiative in this important motion in which she recommends programs to combat sexually transmitted diseases and unwanted pregnancies. Her motion speaks to family planning and also the need for research on safe and effective methods of birth control.
Most of us, if not all on this side of the House, agree with the urgency and the seriousness of these problems but I guess we will differ a little about how we go about solving them.
I would like to make a few remarks. Research in the area of sexual and reproductive health has been identified as a priority by this government. The government is aware that peer and applied research related to the biological and psycho-social aspects of sexual and reproductive health will improve educational programs and service delivery.
It also argues that medical research will improve the present reproductive technologies and will assist in the prevention and treatment of reproductive health problems.
This year a report on adolescent reproductive health, written by a provincial/territorial working group and published by the Department of National health and Welfare, was distributed across Canada. The report outlines recommendations for future action in the area of sexual and reproductive health. The report recognizes reproductive health as an important component of adolescent health and calls for a focus on sexual and reproductive health as a separate field of research.
The adolescent reproductive health working group indicates that the report on the national consultation on research needs and sexuality and reproductive health, a public health perspective, should be used to set priorities. This 1988 report identified and priorized research needed in the field of reproductive health. Twenty five experts from across Canada, sponsored by Health and Welfare Canada, met in Banff, Alberta to develop the report.
The report on adolescent reproductive health acknowledges the existence of inadequate standardization of collection methods and terminology for reproductive health statistics as well as a shortage and inadequate use
of Canadian data on sexual and reproductive health in adolescents. The government is committed to support provinces, territories and organizations to address these research needs identified in the report on adolescent reproductive health.
A major initiative of this government in this area of reproductive health research has been the establishment of the Royal Commission on New Reproductive Technologies. The commission has undertaken a comprehensive research and evaluation program to provide data about the critical analysis of the issues surrounding the new reproductive technologies.
The commission set up a research and evaluation program that will study, among other areas, causes and prevention of infertility. The commission's mandate is broad, involving consideration of social, ethical, health, legal and economic implications of the public's interest. Public input has been considered as extremely important in the over all data collection.
Written submissions as well as many public hearings across Canada have been effective means of gathering this information.
In the spring of 1991 the royal commission released a guide to the research and evaluation program of the Royal Commission on New Reproductive Technologies. This brochure has been extremely popular among members of the research community and the general public. The commission's final report will be completed in the fall of 1992. The recommendations of this royal commission will have a substantial impact on the future directions of research on contraceptive technology and sexual and reproductive health services.
Research results in these areas will also provide Canadians with a greater understanding of safe and effective family planning, methods, and reasons for infertility.
This government's commitment to research in the area of contraception is also evident in the research funded by the National Health Research and Development Program, known as NHRDP.
Since 1986 the government has allocated funding to research through this program, specifically in the area of family planning. NHRDP funded research projects totalled $3.7 million over the last eight years.
October 31, 1991

The research studies have dealt with subjects such as the use of condoms and the pill, adolescent contraceptive practice, vaginal contraceptive devices, and clinical efficacy of the cervical cap. Much of the research focused on aspects of reproductive health other than contraception. Therefore the government made an additional commitment and issued a special call in 1990 for research into family planning, including contraception and problems associated with fertility.
To ensure adequate follow-up the government directed $500,000 a year for the next three years to this special research competition. The research was required to address particular areas of research to be eligible. One of the priorities identified the need to examine the accessibility, availability and acceptability of family planning programs and services to various populations, for example the handicapped, the economically disadvantaged, different cultural groups, and adolescents.
Another area of required research concerns the evaluation of the impact of educational programs, peer counselling models, and the media on sexual practices and contraceptive use.
Finally analysis of the reasons for use or non-use of contraceptives and prevention and effective management of problems related to sub-fertility or infertility is needed.
To this date NHRDP has received 14 proposals. These will be reviewed by a scientific committee in November 1991, just next month, to determine successful research projects.
In summary I again want to compliment the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby. Hopefully together, government and opposition parties, we can make a significant and real headway on these vital social issues.

Mr. Speaker, I am really pleased to be able to speak on this particular motion today. I think back to the very emotionally charged debate on the abortion issue. One of the things I talked about was about my having spoken to a number of women, some who had to go the route of seeking and obtaining an abortion for an unwanted pregnancy and others who made the choice to continue with pregnancy to term, having the child, and then
Private Members' Business
having to deal either with single parenthood in many cases or with giving that child up for adoption.
At that time I emphasized that the answers did not lie with abortions but that women should have the right to choose whether they needed to terminate the pregnancy. What I emphasized over all was that there was a crying need for proper education, for proper funding, for proper facilities and for proper counselling so that particularly young women but not exclusively young women do not have to deal with the horrible choice of whether to terminate the pregnancy or not.
Certainly for the women I have spoken with over the course of my lifetime it is not and never is an easy decision. One way or the other there are psychological ramifications for whatever choice the young woman takes.
I wanted to get up and speak on this motion because I believe that everybody on all sides of the House, and I believe anybody within Canada, would see the good sense in supporting the motion of the member for New Westminster-Burnaby with respect to education on reproductive technology.
Within that motion, and I think it might be beneficial to read it once again into the record, it asks the government:
-to consider the advisability of taking action to reduce the numbers of unwanted pregnancies in our society by reinstating a Family Planning Division at Health and Welfare Canada; reinstating funding to the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada at its previously adequate levels; establishing new programs to combat sexually transmitted diseases and unwanted pregnancies; establishing a national clearinghouse on family planning, and increasing funding for research on safe and effective methods of birth control.
If we look at the the beginning of it we can certainly see the advisability and need for reinstituting the Family Planning Division in Health and Welfare Canada. It is not good enough to say that this is a shared responsibility. I believe that certainly in the western provinces of British Columbia and Saskatchewan we will now see some of these things being dealt with on a provincial level. However I believe the federal government has the primary responsibility for health care and I think it has admitted that to some extent by forming the Royal Commission on Reproductive Technology.

October 31, 1991
Private Members' Business
It should stand up and take that step to ensure that those 66,000 people, usually young women and in some cases older women, who are forced to terminate a pregnancy do not have to take that step in the future. With money properly put into programs for education and counselling, and proper research into reproductive technologies these young women, and in some cases older women, will not have to make that final horrible decision about which way to go.
In my life as a lawyer in British Columbia, I acted for almost 10 years on an ad hoc basis for the Ministry of Social Services and Housing dealing with child paternity suits. I dealt on an ongoing basis with young women, and almost always young women often under the age of 20, who had chosen to have the child but could not bear to give up the child to adoption, to somebody else. By making that decision, unfortunately in almost every case that I dealt with over that 10-year period of time, they were sentenced to a life of poverty.
We did not have the proper and adequate support systems to help these young women. What did they do? Normally they were forced by government policy to sue the father for support. Often the father, in those cases, did not have a good job. He had a low paying job. He was often uneducated and unable to properly and adequately support the child. Yet he was forced to make payments out of his meagre income and the young woman lived a life below the poverty line using the services of social services and housing.
They should not have to make that choice. Those levels of assistance should be there both federally and provincially. As I say it is not adequate to cop out and say it should be done voluntarily or it should be done by the provinces.
The buck stops here. I think it is time that we, as parliamentarians, in the government and on the opposition side began to put our money where our mouth is and say to these people: "We will ensure that we will reduce the number of unwanted pregnancies through the methods set out in this motion".
It is broader than that. I think the statistics presented by the member for New Westminster-Burnaby have pointed out there is and has been a problem of sexually transmitted diseases. All of the speakers have spoken to some extent on that.
We have to bring that level of awareness up within our school system, and I think the parliamentary secretary was correct in saying that we must start at the primary levels to educate the children and talk about sexuality, talk about the consequences of our actions as we grow up and discover our sexuality. I think the point has been very well made that if we do not deal with it now through counselling and services to begin with, the costs into the future are horrendous.
A dollar added now to a program, I believe firmly, will save thousands and thousands of dollars in the years to come on welfare payments, on difficulties with the children in poverty. We now have identified over one million children in poverty. Establishing those programs will also ensure that the problem of sexually transmitted diseases is blocked at the start so that we do not have to pay to assist these people in very expensive hospital care in the the future.
Finally, the government must realize that money put into research is money invested in the future. I implore everybody in the House to support this motion and pass it when it comes up for voting.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate briefly in this debate on the motion from the hon. member for New Westminster- Burnaby.
I thought I was going to be allowed ten minutes, but I realize that I have barely two minutes, so it will be very difficult for me to say everything I expected to say on the subject.
Like my colleague for Argenteuil-Papineau, I would first congratulate the hon. member for Westminster- Burnaby on having made this issue the subject of a debate in the House. It is a very important subject and we all know how active the hon. member is on social issues, the statut of women, and so on. So I congratulate her.
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in saying that the government has taken many initiatives; I cannot list them all, but there are a lot. There is for instance the creation of the Sexually Transmitted Diseases Division, at the National Laboratory for Sexually Transmitted Disease Control, as well as other initiatives. Mr. Speaker, I see you are telling me that my time is up. I was

extremely pleased to have an opportunity to elaborate on such an important issue.

Mr. Speaker, the previous motion will come back for two more hours of debate. Some of the members on the other side may be interested in knowing that.
I asked a question some time ago about whether Canada would honour its own commitment to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which clearly requires the government to ensure the development of institutions, services and facilities for the care of children whose parents are working outside the home.
Sadly the response I received was inadequate. The Minister of National Health and Welfare simply stated that his government came up with a proposal in 1988 and that the Senate turned it down. In fact, the senators never had an opportunity to turn it down. The Prime Minister called an election a few hours before the bill was to be voted on in the Senate, in one of the most manipulative manoeuvres I have ever seen. But the bill itself was not even a good one. At the time, it looked even worse than simply continuing under the Canada Assistance Plan, which is how child care in this country is currently funded.
Adjournment Debate
That was before this government capped the Canada Assistance Plan for the provinces of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
There is a child care crisis in this country. Almost three million Canadian children require child care. There are only 300,000 regulated child care spaces in the entire country. The minister tried to sidetrack the question by claiming to be spending $136 million on child poverty and on violence.
But it is a funny thing, every time I ask a question in this House, that same $136 million keeps popping up. It is supposed to be for women, and then it is supposed to be for seniors, and then it is supposed to be for aboriginals and then it is supposed to be for child care. In fact, it is not $136 million, it is $49 million that will be spent before the next election that is supposed to solve just about every social problem we have in this country. A lot of that money is going to research.
We do not need more research. We know what the problem is. We need action. What is more, not a single red cent of that money is going to eliminate child poverty.
We hear over and over again from the other side of the House that you cannot just throw money at a problem. The people who say that have enough to eat. They have jobs. They are not the people who line up at food banks, who cannot get job training. They are not the battered women with children who are turned away from shelters because of a lack of space.
In fact the Tory reduction of funds to the Canada Assistance Plan amounts to more than $155 million over the next two years. It funds programs to help poor people to get back on their feet. It helps families of poor children. Some 37 per cent of all welfare recipients are children. The lack of affordable child care is a barrier for people looking for jobs. Fifty per cent of Canada's poor live in the three affected provinces. The poor in these provinces are just as poor as those in other provinces in Canada. The children who need child care in those provinces are in just as much need as the children in other provinces. This government is playing political games with people's lives.
The second part of the question I asked dealt with how Canada was going to keep the commitment that it made to the UN on a child's right to health care and education

Adjournment Debate
services. How can it do this when it has cut back already on these services?
The minister's response was that we had to consider Canada's ability to pay. That is just fine. Why did this government not consider Canada's capacity to pay before it made that commitment to the UN? Why did the government make a commitment it had no intention of keeping?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly proud to speak this evening to reply to two points raised in this adjournment motion by the hon. member. First, as regards the United Nation Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Prime Minister clearly said this week that he thought that the provinces which must ratify the convention before the federal government should do so by year's end. The Prime Minister also told the House that, in his opinion, there was no doubt that the convention would be ratified within the timeframe to which we are committed.
As for me, I sent the complete text to all the churches and elementary schools in my riding to remind my constituents that a convention had been signed, because it is extremely important that all the people in our ridings know about this. As you know, Mr. Speaker, each and every one of us must do something about the issue of daycare.
Do you know what I did? In 1988,1 held a meeting for business people from the St. Janvier region, in Mirabel. I convinced them that daycare also concerned them. And do you know what happened? Through the national Child Care Initiative Fund, we were able to finance a small study that cost $25,000, and the province of Quebec, through I'Agence de garde en milieu familial, provided 60 daycare spaces. Moreover, with the help of three large companies, Bombardier (Canadair Division-Military Aircraft), Bell Helicopter and Air Trans-at, and the City of Mirabel, we opened a daycare facility for 60 children last week, thanks to the initiative of your humble servant in this House. It is a unique concept in the work place in Canada. I invite hon. members to do the same, because I think this is an example that could be followed across the country. Because we were able to get daycare spaces for 120 children, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that.

Mr. Speaker, when is a cap not a cap? When it is ethereal, a gaseous vapour, a hovering mist dissipating and reforming in mysterious and unpredictable fashion. The government claims to be firmly committed to capping Canada's emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases at 1990 levels, by the year 2000. Unfortunately, upon close examination this commitment which seems not just firm but rock solid, vaporises into some ghostly, shifting ethereal mist.
There are three ways in which this commitment is less substantial than most people think. First, there is good evidence that the government's commitment applies to net emissions, not to gross emissions. Page 102 of the green plan indicates that the government is considering action to limit net emissions of greenhouse gases. The reference to net emissions is repeated in Canada's intervention to an international climate change convention on September 18, 1991 in Nairobi, Kenya.
The apparent insistence on net emissions could be very important. It is a rather straightforward task to compile an inventory, as Environment Canada currently does, of gross emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. It is much more complicated to estimate both sources and sinks for these gases. Canadian estimates could very well be tied up in scientific controversy even as we approach the year 2000 and the cap from a practical standpoint will have been useless.
Even if Canada decides to make monitoring easier and caps gross carbon dioxide emissions, that commitment remains vague because within the government there seems to be no agreement on how much CO2 was emitted in 1990. In the national action strategy on global warming the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment estimated 1990 emissions at 467 megatons. A document dated July 18, 1990, issued by the energy and fiscal analysis division of Energy, Mines and Resources, offers an estimate of 508 megatons. The National Energy Board's June 1991 estimate for 1990 CO2 emissions is 517 megatons. These three government
October 31, 1991

estimates for Canadian 1990 carbon dioxide emissions differ by 11 per cent. This is hardly precise for a cap. However there is a third problem. According to a senior government official, 1990 might not mean 1990 after all.
On October 3, 1991,1 asked the deputy minister of the environment: "Is it reasonable to assume that the 1990 emissions level will not absolutely and without variance be the basis used for comparison by the year 2000? Is it possible that it might change as a consequence of international negotiations and of methodologies within the country?"
The deputy minister, Dr. Good, replied: "It is quite possible". So the government's own estimates for carbon dioxide are significantly divergent. Small wonder then that few people seem to take the government's commitment seriously.
My question is clear and simple. When the government says it wants to cap CO2 and other greenhouse gas emissions at their 1990 levels by the year 2000, what in heaven's name does it mean?

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government remains to committed to stabilizing the emissions of CO2 and other greenhouse gases at 1990 levels by the year 2000.
Our efforts to address the issue of global warming are taking place at both the national and international levels. Internationally, Canada has participated in intergovernmental negotiations and framework conventions on climate change. It is important that Canada act in concert with the international community on what is after all a global issue.
On the national front, the federal government's commitment to address climate change is clearly spelled out in Canada's green plan. We are pursuing a comprehensive, flexible approach to limiting net emissions of greenhouse gases, addressing both sources and "sinks", while at the same time acknowledging regional differences.
Carbon dioxide is one of the main greenhouse gases, and most man-made CO2 comes comes from our consumption of fossil fuels. Consequently my department is developing a series of initiatives to promote energy efficiency as a cost effective way to reducing energy
Adjournment Debate
consumption and CO2 emissions. Measures will be announced in due course to regulate minimum efficiency levels in energy using equipment, to label products regarding their energy use, promote more energy efficient building codes and to initiate a further round of fuel efficiency targets for new vehicles. These are but a few initiatives at the federal level.
The accelerated development and market penetration of alternative motive fuels, as well as research and development of alternative energy is also being pursued. In addition, we shall be initiating information and education campaigns for the public on the wise use of energy. These, along with other measures yet to be announced, are an indication that this government is committed to taking action to meet our stabilization goal.
Provincial and territorial governments, as well as municipalities have important roles to play. Many provinces have undertaken measures to limit CO2 and other greenhouse gas emissions. Others are planning to do so. My government is pursuing discussions with the provinces and territories on this matter in order to better co-ordinate actions and share information and data.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to stand here and to again ask for answers to the question I asked of both the Secretary of State for Canada and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Specifically I was trying to learn from the Government of Canada what steps it would take in honouring and moving to honour the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
I listened very carefully to the parliamentary secretary who responded a moment ago. Although Canada has certainly indicated its interest, and has signed the agreement at the United Nations on the Rights of the Child, it still has not ratified it. Many countries around the world have ratified it.
My question was simply to ask why this was not happening.
In addition to that, I have also written to the Minister for External Relations and International Development. I had asked these questions in the House, and I had written, and still, I am not any closer to getting an answer. What I really need to know is what steps the government still has to take before honouring this

Adjournment Debate
agreement. I want to know about the process for ratifying this agreement and these are the answers that I need.
The facts on the convention are that just over a year ago representatives of a 159 nations around the world gathered at the United Nations to begin the process of ending child poverty world-wide. It is interesting to hear the member for Burnaby in her private member's motion talking about child poverty and then her adjournment proceedings with regard to the rights of the child.
There is incredible child poverty, not only in this country but around the world. The summit's main goal was to encourage governments to sign and ratify this agreement. The convention is committed to recognizing the right of every child to a standard of living adequate for the child's physical, mental, spiritual, moral and social development.
As I review Hansard over the last few months I note that every time the government is asked about the convention's ratification it becomes defensive or, in my case, each time that I have posed questions it refuses to answer.
There is reason to believe that Canada will have trouble ratifying the convention because several areas of minimum standards for children, including health, health care and education, fall under provincial jurisdiction.
The federal government has put a cap on the Canada Assistance Plan which pays for many of the programs needed by impoverished people, the majority of whom are children.
This week the Child Welfare League of Canada, the Canadian Welfare Association, and the Canadian Council of Children and Youth held a national symposium in Ottawa to review the state of Canada's children and youth as it relates to the UN convention. At the closing of the symposium they stated that the Canadian government's disastrous social and economic policies have turned child poverty into a national scandal.
One of the conference organizers, Patrick Johnston, said it best when he said: "We are getting tired of hearing reasons why kids cannot be made a priority. We deal with the Constitution. We deal with interest rates, but we never talk about Canada's children. "One in six children lives in poverty. Poor children experience a 50
per cent higher death rate from all causes. Poor children are more than twice as likely to suffer long-term disability and other health problems. The average life expectancy for aboriginal children, for example, is eight years lower than the national average. The high school drop-out rate is more than 90 per cent in some parts of the country for poor children."
Surely if other countries around the world can ratify this agreement then Canada can. We know it probably will be costly. But, for goodness sake, let us get on with it. I and others in this House are very tired of asking why, when, and how, and we have yet to receive an adequate response.
We are all on the side of children I would hope in this House of Commons. I am not attacking the government. I just want an answer, Mr. Speaker, thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to ask my question again.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all know that the Convention on the Rights of the Child at the United Nations was an historic event and the culmination of almost 10 years of discussions that began shortly after the International Year of the Child in 1979.
The member knows very well that many of the convention articles apply directly to provincial and territorial governments and the services they provide.
Aware of this reality and within the human rights tradition of the Government of Canada, steps were taken in 1982 to establish a federal-provincial-territorial committee of human rights officials to provide full Canadian input into the drafting of the conventions and, more recent, to review federal and provincial law to ensure Canadian compliance with the convention. This process has been thorough, consultative and successful.
I am informed, as I said earlier, that the final stages of the review are almost completed. Governments have been asked to signify formally their support for the ratification by the Government of Canada of the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Much has been made recently of the observation that Canada has not yet ratified the convention, the implication being that the Government of Canada might be delaying or purposely avoiding ratification. This is not the case. It was never the case. In fact the reverse is true.
October 31, 1991

Canada's commitment to the ratification of the convention has never wavered, nor has our policy to work closely and in collaboration with provincial and territorial governments with a substantial stake in the convention.
I know the member would like the Government of Canada to overrule provincial obligation and responsibilities, but we do not.

Mr. Speaker, for over 30 years EFL Furs International was a thriving and a growing manufacturing business.
Its founder, my friend Simos Papadopoulos, came to Canada from Greece with virtually nothing. Through his hard work and the hard work of his family, his late wife, his two sons, Harry and Peter, built a thriving and a very prosperous business which employed close to 100 people. It developed a very significant export trade for Canada in the United States and in Asia. It paid very substantial taxes and provided the basis which allowed the Papadopoulos family to participate in a great many volunteer organizations and charitable organizations in the wider community which did all of us an enormous amount of good.
Now EFL is gone. It has gone bankrupt and the Papadopoulos family has been wiped out. It did not miss an interest payment on its bank loan, but the bank called its loan anyway. Simos voluntarily mortgaged his own home and put all that money into the business. The bank took the money and Simos lost his own home.
Harry sold his home. He put his money into the business on a voluntary basis. The bank took his money and now Harry and his family have been left without a house.
They asked the government for help, for a temporary loan, not for a grant, and the government let them down. They prepared a business plan to show how they could pay off all of their debts. "No", said the bank, "we would rather lose millions of dollars than give you a little more time".
Perhaps EFL and the many families which relied on it for their living, for their jobs that provided them with
Adjournment Debate
their living, could have been saved if we had only had in place a U.S.-style chapter 11 bankruptcy law.
The formal Liberal government promised a law of that sort some six times over a period of 25 years and our own government promised that sort of a law in the 1989 Speech from the Throne. Finally this past June a bill of this sort was introduced in the House, Bill C-22. It is now before the House for its second reading.
If we are going to prevent any more tragedies, like the tragedy that happened to EFL, if we are going to prevent any more tragedies like the tragedy that has happened to the Papadopoulos family and so many other like families, we have to get on with passing this legislation and passing it as quickly as possible.
Tonight I want to call on the minister to ensure that this bill gets passed just as quickly as possible and gets put into place at least by January 1, 1992 so that we will never again have a tragedy like the one that happened to EFL and the Papadopoulos family.
Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State
(Finance)): Mr. Speaker, on June 13 of this year, to overwhelming stakeholder interest and applause, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs introduced Bill C-22, the reforms to the Bankruptcy Act.
This new legislation is the result of extensive consultation with provincial and territorial governments, labour, business, consumers, legal and insolvency experts. This government knows that saving business means saving jobs.
Accordingly, the focus of this bill is on rehabilitation, not on liquidation. By making reorganization provisions more flexible and more accessible, the reform package provides a greater latitude for debtors to get back on their feet. The new act will strengthen the Canadian business to make it more competitive. The new act also is an important initiative for other segments of the Canadian economy. It will provide greater protection for the most vulnerable participants in the economy, the wage earners, consumers and unpaid suppliers.
Wage earners will be guaranteed a minimal level of protection for the recovery of moneys owed to them in bankruptcies. The program will be accessible, user-friendly, and designed to put cash in their pockets. The Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act will give consumers an opportunity to negotiate arrangements with creditors in

Adjournment Debate
order to avoid bankruptcy and start all over again. That is what my colleague is talking about with his friends in the fur industry.
The reforms offer broader protection for unsecured creditors. Unpaid suppliers will be given the right within 30 days to reclaim goods from a firm that is subsequently declared bankrupt.
The new bill offers flexible, modern rules that recognize natural market forces. It is an important element in the framework that will allow this government to foster a competitive, productive and national economy.
We feel that in giving viable enterprises the chance to reorganize we can avoid many bankruptcies and save thousands of jobs and avoid losing the expertise essential to encourage Canadian competitiveness.

Others may recall that on June 17 I stood in this House and asked a question of the Secretary of State with regard to the kinds of protections that might be given official minority language groups. There were rumours at the time that the government might be thinking of changing that.
I am here this evening to quote the response and to raise a few questions. For example, part of the response says, and I quote: "his government was standing for the rights of linguistic minorities outside and inside Quebec". When people heard that they said: "Where was the government when Bill 178, the sign law, was passed?" Some questions were raised. What was it able to do? Where was the government? Was anything said about this poor elderly gentleman? He was around 65 years old I believe and was the bus driver who was dismissed even though he had driven the bus for 18 years. Apparently he was not able to speak the language sufficiently for the students. He was dismissed in spite of the fact that the parents supported him, the parents wanted him. Where was the government, for example, when the French language rights in Saskatchewan and Alberta, just a few years ago, were diminished significantly?
When the government says it is standing for the rights of linguistic minorities outside and inside Quebec, people are just a little nervous. They ask: "Where is the government with respect to the Supreme Court decision that says that French language groups outside of Quebec
should have governance over their educational systems?"
There is a second part of the answer that I want to address, and it is referring to the govemment:"It is a commitment that we maintain and it is a commitment that we will respect in years to come", that is with respect to the protection of minority language groups.
Some of you will know that in current constitutional proposals there is a reference to the preservation and promotion of the distinct society. I have no particular difficulty with that. I understand the desire of people to want to do that. Those same words were there in the Meech Lake Accord with respect to the minority language groups. Now we know with respect to minority language groups, the French language group, that the only word that is there is "preservation". Why has "promotion" been dropped? Was it an accident?

Nothing is more sensitive or touchy than this language issue, and one really has to be careful. As you know, there was an incident last week. Some young aboriginal hockey players wanted to go to Quebec, but were apparently not allowed or accepted in French-speaking homes. I tried to talk to both sides in order to find out who was right. I still have not found the answer, but I can tell you that this issue generated a lot of calls.
It is a sensitive issue and one must tread very carefully. That is why I asked the question; I said that the national government must protect its minorities. We must know where it stands on this issue. We need leadership. If it is not done for these minority groups, others will also be afraid.
I am trying to be very, very reasonable and I request an answer.

Mr. Speaker, I went to a meeting with the Federation des parents francophones in Winnipeg, in the hon. member's riding I believe, in St. Boniface.

Brian Mulroney, for saying that he supported and stood behind Franco-Manitobans in their struggle, in 1984, after the Supreme Court's decision on the province's statutes. The hon. member knows perfectly well that the Conservative

government and the Prime Minister enjoy great respect in Manitoba, in his riding.
Mr. Speaker, the reform of the Official Languages Act is the best indication of this government's commitment and vision with respect to the interests and concerns of official language groups.
Our commitment goes further, Mr. Speaker. As partners sharing the same values, the federal government, the provinces and the territories have concluded new bilateral agreements on minority language education and second language education. We have also signed co-operative agreements with nine provinces and territories, to promote an increase in minority language services. We have also increased support for organizations and institutions in official language communities.
The hon. member alluded to a minor problem that occurred in connection with children who wanted to play
Adjournment Debate
hockey in Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member either had a poor interpretation or perhaps misunderstood, because that is what often happens. People tend to misread the facts.
